I built three different DIY solar panel mounting systems around my solar shed in Florida, and each one solves a different problem.

In this video, I walk through hinged vertical solar panels, adjustable fence-mounted panels, temporary yard stake mounts, seasonal panel angles, storm preparation, and what I learned from testing different mounting methods in the real world.

One of the biggest challenges with solar in Florida is balancing solar production, hurricane preparation, easy maintenance, cost, and adjustable panel angles. Instead of building one giant permanent system, I experimented with several lower-cost mounting methods that can be folded down, adjusted seasonally, temporarily removed, or upgraded later.

☀️ WHAT YOU’LL SEE

- Hinged vertical solar panels
- Adjustable fence-mounted solar panels
- Temporary yard stake solar mounts
- Seasonal solar panel angles
- Florida hurricane preparation
- Temporary vs. permanent solar systems
- Wire management and cable safety
- Quick disconnection for storm prep
- Ground mounts vs. fence mounts
- Commercial mounting alternatives
- Beginner recommendations
- Real-world lessons learned

🌪️ WHY THIS MATTERS IN FLORIDA

Solar panel mounts are not just about getting the best angle.

In Florida, you also have to think about wind, hurricanes, storms, maintenance, yard access, panel cleaning, wire safety, and whether your system can be secured or removed before bad weather.

A mount that produces great power but is difficult to service or impossible to storm prep may not be the best solution for every DIY solar build.

That is why I tested several mounting ideas around the solar shed instead of relying on only one method.

🔧 MOUNTING OPTIONS DISCUSSED

- Hinged fence-mounted panels that can fold down
- Ground-mounted panels using simple stakes
- 2x4 fixed-angle fence mounts
- Commercial ground rack options
- Ballast rack systems
- Adjustable A-frame mounts
- Roof and fence tilt brackets
- Simple Z-brackets for RVs and sheds

Each option has trade-offs. Some are cheaper and easier to modify. Some are more permanent and professional. Some are better for storm prep, while others are better for long-term stability.

snippet.title: Live: Top 10 Hurricane Prep Mistakes Solar Owners Make  📱
snippet.description:
Hurricane season is here, and a lot of solar owners may not be nearly as ready as they think.

In this livestream, we are going through the Top 10 Hurricane Prep Mistakes Solar Owners Make — from assuming rooftop solar works during a grid outage, to not having battery backup, no transfer switch, no critical-load plan, no fuel plan, and not testing the system before the storm is already on the way.

Most rooftop solar systems are grid-tied, and many still do not include battery backup. Wood Mackenzie reported that the U.S. residential solar-plus-storage attachment rate reached 25% in Q1 2024, which means roughly 75% of new residential solar installs at that time were still solar-only. If the grid goes down, many of those systems will shut down unless they are designed with backup power in mind.

Tonight we’ll talk about:
• Why solar panels alone may not power your house during an outage
• The biggest battery backup mistakes
• Generator vs battery backup planning
• Critical loads and what you really need to keep running
• Transfer switches, interlocks, and safe power transfer
• Internet, communications, and monitoring during outages
• Spare parts, extension cords, fuel, and storm timing
• What I would do differently before a hurricane

This livestream is meant to help homeowners, DIY solar users, RV owners, and anyone thinking about backup power build a safer and more realistic storm plan.

Next week we’ll continue the conversation with a roundtable livestream featuring other YouTubers talking about their disaster recovery plans, solar backup systems, storm prep, and how they would handle hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, snowstorms, and long-term outages.
